title: Source generators (compile-time code, not run-time magic)
hook: Source generators run during compilation and add C# source files to your project — turning attributes or syntax into strongly typed code. They replace slow reflection for serializers, dependency injection glue, and Platform Invoke (P/Invoke) wrappers.

blocks.text: IIncrementalGenerator (Roslyn source generator API) inspects your compilation and emits partial classes, methods, or entire files. Generated code appears in obj/ and compiles with your project — you debug it like hand-written code. Examples: System.Text.Json source context, logging MessagePack, LibraryImport for P/Invoke, community generators for records and unions.

entries.plainDefinition: Compile-time plugin that adds C# source based on your code.
Modern generator API that caches steps for faster rebuilds.
entries.example: Implement IIncrementalGenerator in an analyzer project.

entries.plainDefinition: Type split across multiple files; generator adds another part.
entries.example: partial class OrderDto { } // other part generated

blocks.text: SQS consumers that deserialized JSON via reflection per message can switch to source-generated System.Text.Json context for faster, trim-safe code. Generators eliminate stringly typed method names and catch errors at compile time. They are the .NET answer to TypeScript codegen from OpenAPI — but embedded in the build.

blocks.title: Generator vs reflection
blocks.body: If you need the same metadata-driven code on every request, generate it once at compile time.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Editing generated files manually — they regenerate on build. Generator project not referenced as analyzer. Debugging without looking at generated .g.cs in obj folder.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: source generators run at compile time — zero per-request cost. Inspect obj/generated for .g.cs output when debugging. IIncrementalGenerator caches syntax steps for faster rebuilds on large solutions. DynamicallyAccessedMembers annotates reflection entry points so trimming and Native AOT preserve required metadata; without roots, publish succeeds but runtime throws MissingMethodException. Prefer JsonSerializerContext over reflection serializers on SQS hot paths — measurable CPU drop in dotnet-counters.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Calling source generators 'macros' without mentioning Roslyn IIncrementalGenerator. Ignoring DynamicallyAccessedMembers when claiming reflection works with Native AOT. Editing .g.cs files in obj. Not knowing generators execute in the analyzer process — they cannot access run-time Redis or file I/O.

interviewTakeaways: Source generators emit C# during compilation via IIncrementalGenerator — no runtime reflection cost on hot paths.
DynamicallyAccessedMembers roots types for trimmers and Native AOT when limited reflection remains necessary.
In production, compare CPU on SQS deserialize before/after JsonSerializerContext — generators win on volume.
60s: Generators add .g.cs at compile time. JsonSerializerContext and LibraryImport are built-in. Use DynamicallyAccessedMembers for trim-safe reflection. Never edit generated files.
Follow-up: how does IIncrementalGenerator differ from the old ISourceGenerator API?
commonPitfalls: Hand-editing generated .g.cs files gets you rejected — changes vanish on next build.
Reflection serializer on hot path without trim annotations — Native AOT publish breaks silently at runtime.
Strong answer: 'Generator for compile-time code. DynamicallyAccessedMembers for remaining reflection. Profile deserialize CPU after switching from reflection.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: openapi-typescript and similar tools mirror source generators — schema drives generated types and clients at build time.
Webpack/babel plugins emit helper code at build time like Roslyn generators, but JS still interprets or JITs the output — C# generators feed the same Roslyn compile to IL.
